title: Marketing essentials
blurb: The ideas every marketer uses, from the four Ps to lifetime value.

cards.text: The marketing mix, or four Ps, is a classic way to plan how you take something to market. E. Jerome McCarthy popularised it in 1960.
What you sell and the problem it solves: its features, quality, design and packaging.
What customers pay, how that compares with rivals, and the value they feel they get. Price also signals quality.
Place is where and how people can buy. Promotion is how they hear about you: advertising, PR, social media and sales.
For services, three more are often added: people, process and physical evidence.

cards.q: Which is NOT one of the original four Ps?
cards.explain: People was added later, in the seven Ps for services.

points: Services add people, process and physical evidence

cards.text: Market segmentation splits a market into groups of people with shared needs, so you can serve each group better.
Common bases are demographic (age, income), geographic (where people live), psychographic (values, lifestyle) and behavioural (how people buy and use).
Then choose which segments to focus on, weighing their size, their growth and how well you can serve them.
Positioning is the place you want to hold in customers’ minds compared with rivals: the cheapest, the safest or the most premium, for example.
Together it’s called STP: segment, target, position. It comes before you decide the four Ps.

points: Split the market into groups with shared needs
Pick the groups you can serve best
Decide how you want them to see you

cards.text: One of the oldest models of how people buy: attention, interest, desire, action. It’s credited to advertising pioneer E. St. Elmo Lewis in the 1890s.
It’s often drawn as a funnel: many people become aware of you, fewer consider you, and fewer still buy. Each stage needs a different message.
If 1,000 people visit a page and 30 sign up, the conversion rate is 3%.
Measuring each stage shows where people drop out, so you can fix the weakest step instead of just shouting louder at the top.

cards.q: 1,000 visitors and 30 sign-ups. What’s the conversion rate?

points: Fewer people reach each stage of the funnel
Find and fix where people drop out

cards.text: Winning a new customer usually costs more than keeping one you already have, so strong businesses look after existing customers.
Customer relationship management is the practice, and the software, for keeping track of every interaction with customers, from first contact to repeat purchase.
Customer lifetime value estimates what a customer is worth over the whole relationship. It helps decide how much to spend winning and keeping them.
NPS asks how likely customers are to recommend you, from 0 to 10. The score is the percentage of 9s and 10s minus the percentage of 0s to 6s.

cards.q: In NPS, who counts as a promoter?
cards.explain: Only 9s and 10s. 7s and 8s are passives; 0 to 6 are detractors.

points: Keeping customers usually beats finding new ones
Lifetime value and NPS show how you’re doing
